paragraphs.text: This leaf grew in [Anxi](anxi:where-it-is), a county of southern Fujian in Quanzhou prefecture, on the southern side of the Daiyun mountains, where [Tieguanyin](anxi:known-for) fills most of the tea land. The county is warm, wet and misty, and its hills of [weathered granite](anxi:why-tea) break down into acidic red and yellow soil that drains freely, which is why tea does well there.

[Tieguanyin](tieguanyin:definition) is the name of a cultivar and of the [oolong](oolong:definition) made from it, a partly oxidised tea. Once the leaf is shaken, fixed and rolled, it goes through [cloth wrap rolling](tieguanyin:making): it is wrapped, pressed and dried a little, over and over, and each round draws it tighter into the balls it keeps here. This one was then made into a [scented tea](tieguanyin:osmanthus): fresh osmanthus flowers were layered through the finished tea, and the tea was dried once more.

brewing.text: Tieguanyin is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C; the light green style is often taken a little cooler, about 85 to 95°C. Use about 4 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 150 ml gaiwan or pot, about a third full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 10 to 30 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and a good Tieguanyin gives about six to eight. In a larger pot, use about 2.5 to 5 grams for 240 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: In the light style: orchid and other flowers, a fresh, clean cup and a sweet aftertaste. In the roasted style: toast and charcoal, caramel or honey, stone or dried fruit, nuts, and a liquor that runs from gold to amber.
